source.title: record: ripr-swarm measurement ledger (steward, measured detail behind the direction record)

labels.name: status/done-open
labels.description: Delivered; the issue is intentionally kept open.

source.body:
**This is the measurement ledger for the ripr-swarm direction record (#14633). It is an evidence store, not a direction document.** The direction record holds accepted intent, product boundaries, durable sequencing constraints, strategic trade-offs and genuinely open decisions. This ledger holds the measurements those rules rest on: dated, with population, analyzer revision and surface named where the figure carries one. Nothing here is a new claim; each block is the measured text that was in the record, moved verbatim on 2026-11-15 so a fresh session can reach the decisions in minutes and follow a link when it needs the numbers.

Reading rule, taken from the record and unchanged: a product figure carries the population, the analyzer revision and the surface that produced it. A figure naming two of the three is ambiguous, and the ambiguity has so far run in the direction that flatters the product. Where a block below is stale, it is stale-not-green - the record's staleness rule, not a licence to quote it.

Contents: (A) join coverage and the seam vocabulary; (B) calibration population, precision and receipts; (C) adoption evidence; (D) surfaces, bars and the December verdict; (E) the editor action surface; (F) gate and landing-path corroboration.

---

## (A) Join coverage and the seam vocabulary

### The join-coverage bar is a capability bar, not a repair bar (measured 2026-11-14; receipt identity corrected 2026-11-14T16:49Z)

The public page carries one bar that decides whether the calibration number describes the product or a quarter of it: `trust.mutation_join_coverage`, target 0.5, now 0.283 (493 of 1,745 mutants). **That 1,745 / 493 / 827 trio is the five-crate receipt** (run 43384486566, analyzer `f5f65dd`; rust-hex, semver, strsim-rs, bytesize, humantime), not the frozen twelve-crate boundary. The all-twelve-selected run (43389621057) scores nine repositories at **2,360 mutants, 620 canonical-precise (26.3%) and 1,058 with no containing seam**. Neither subset is the completed calibration result.

The 827 no-containing-seam mutants of the five-crate slice are classified, all of them (Research Brief 42, recorded on #12901):

| class | count | share of the 827 classified (five-crate) | what it needs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| true join gaps | 39 | 4.7% | a bounded repair |
| FnValue whole-function replacements | 170 | 20.6% | an operator-scope/claim change |
| intermediate expressions in owners that already have seams | 604 | 73.0% | an expression-level seam model |
| no seam in the owner | 14 | 1.7% | out of scope |

Arithmetic on the five-crate slice: widening the join recovers at most 39, which is 30.5% - still below the bar. The 604 class, if every one qualified, is 62.9% - above it. **Both are conditional scenarios, not measured recoveries.** The owner's 14:12Z clarification on #14711 adds two limits: the per-record 39/170/604/14 partition was not independently inspected, and the current score contract restricts genres, seam kinds and outcomes, so "the 604 would become eligible canonical-precise records" is not established. The 425 other unmatched dispositions in the all-twelve receipt are unclassified. **No path to the 50% bar is established at the twelve-crate boundary.**

What is established is narrower and still material: the seam vocabulary (`SeamKind`: `predicate_boundary`, `error_variant`, `return_value`, `field_construction`, `side_effect`, `match_arm`, `call_presence`) has no expression-level kind, so intermediate-expression behavior in owners that already have seams is unrepresentable, and on the five-crate slice that class is large enough that repair alone cannot reach 50%.

Two consequences for sequencing, neither of them a ruling:

- The bar cannot be met by repair work on the five-crate slice, and moving it would be re-baselining - the trap this record already names. A bar that only a new capability can reach is a capability bar, and it should be read as a statement about the instrument, not a backlog item.
- The record's own order is characterize, then change the instrument, then measure the population. Characterization is done on one five-crate slice, not on the twelve-crate boundary. The instrument change is a candidate next step, and its design carrier is #14711 (opened 2026-11-14T14:04Z, unassigned); the claim-granularity decision it depends on is open decision 6 below and is the owner's. A carrier is not an owner: the design does not start until that decision is made, and the November window is the constraint, because the non-goal forbids architecture migration during the December measurement month. The decision now has a corrected premise: not "the only path", but "a large unrepresentable class, with no boundary-level path established".

## (B) Calibration population, precision and receipts

- **Calibration premise is not yet met on the repo's own crate (measured 2026-11-14).** The #14116 composed replay was run on current main `db01ef5618` (binary built from that tree) over the same eight merged commits, one commit at a time (`--base <sha>~1 --committed`): **198 probes, 1 `exposed` (0.5%), 94 `weakly_exposed` (47%), 4 `reachable_unrevealed`, 78 `static_unknown` (39%), 8 `infection_unknown`, 13 `propagation_unknown`.** The headline is unchanged from the pre-fix 1 of 199. The #14062 finding is still `weakly_exposed` with `assert_eq!` not credited because `use rayon::prelude::*;` at `crates/ripr/src/analysis/classify/owner_pin.rs:101` is read as workspace-wide. The root cause is `crates/ripr/src/analysis/scip/mod.rs:14` `include!("generated/scip.rs")` inside `pub mod scip`: the fragment declares only inline `pub mod descriptor` / `pub mod symbol_information`, so it mounts no other file, yet `is_file_level == false` records `rust_include_nested_module_context` and disables placement for the whole crate. The #14116 acceptance ("credits exact assert_eq! oracles in tests whose own crate has no unplaced include") therefore cannot be demonstrated on `crates/ripr` tests, which is where the eight PRs' changes live. The lever is a bounded rule change: a nested include whose fragment mounts nothing (inline mods only) is placeable; one that mounts a file stays refused. Until that lands, or the owner rules that the workspace-wide scope stays with fixed disclosure, the calibration campaign's first slice measures the known defect, not the product.

- A calibration population must contain code the instrument did not write. A number taken from the analyzer's own repair surface measures whether the repair is covered, not whether the product discriminates. Those are different claims with different acceptance boundaries, and a repair gate promoted to a calibration slice is a self-measurement dressed as a product result.
- **The precision problem is the owner tier (measured 2026-11-14, carrier #12901).** Pinned pilot-ranking corpus 2026-10-04.1 records top-10 6 confirmed and 10 refuted of 30 picks, top-5 2 and 7 of 15; by tier seam 6/6 confirmed, line 0/0, owner 0/10 at top-10 and seam 2/2, owner 0/7 at top-5. The seam tier is not the weakness, and growing the corpus without splitting the tiers would let a perfect seam rate sit beside a zero owner rate in one pooled number. Leading indicator, not a decision: whether owner-tier picks stay ranked while they read 0 of 10 confirmed is a product-boundary call, not a delivery one. The split is not a single-morning artifact: it is the committed corpus version, and the live "7 / 9 of 9 / 0 of 17" figures that previously appeared here are withdrawn because no committed receipt carries them. A `pass` on that board is also not a fake-clean to be alarmed at: the nine metrics are measured (7 `below_target`, 2 `meets_target`), the `not_measured` statuses belong to the per-repo rows rather than the metrics, and the gate is a no-regression gate whose board status already reads `gaps`.
- **A public calibration figure is a receipt, and receipt staleness is invisible to the drift guard (measured 2026-11-14).** `metrics/public-proof/mutation-spot-check.json` was produced by analyzer `731e36e` (2026-10-17) and committed 2026-11-05; main is now >3,400 commits ahead of that analyzer (3,458 at main `7188886`, 2026-11-14T23:49Z). `cargo xtask public-proof --check` compares the page against the committed receipts, so a stale receipt agrees with its own stale page and the guard stays green. A manually dispatched refresh on 2026-11-13 over the same five crates and byte-identical mutant sets (`mutant_set_sha256` equal for all five) with analyzer `f5f65dd` (2026-11-12) reads precision 95.4% (62/65, 3 overclaims) against the published 96.8% (61/63, 2), recall-of-missed 63.2% against 58.7%, strict ungripped share 26.2% against 10.6%, scored coverage unchanged at 28.3%, and no-containing-seam 47.4% against 48.3%. The published receipt's only met criterion (time vs full cargo-mutants) is `not_established` in the batch, because a batch records no paired timing. The movement is a recall-for-precision trade, not a pure regression; either way the published page is not a current measurement, and this drift runs in the flattering direction. Rule: a product figure carries the analyzer revision that produced it; when the instrument has moved since the receipt, the receipt is stale-not-green whatever the page says. A refresh lane with no schedule cannot keep a product claim current, and a drift guard whose surface is page-versus-receipt cannot see the receipt.

- **The next campaign's dominant quantity is join coverage, not precision (measured 2026-11-14 on the 2026-11-13 receipt; characterized 2026-11-14).** On the five-crate receipt, 493 of 1,745 mutants (28.3%) reach a canonical_precise seam join and 827 (47.4%) have no containing seam at all; the twelve-crate boundary receipt reads 620 of 2,360 (26.3%) joined and 1,058 unmatched. Precision over the scored subset is 95.4-96.8%, so "precision is nearly at the bar" describes the quarter of the mutation surface the instrument can see. The characterization question this bullet used to leave open is answered for the five-crate slice only: 73.0% of its 827 no-seam records is intermediate-expression behavior in owners that already have seams, 20.6% is whole-function replacement, 4.7% is a true join gap and 1.7% has no seam in the owner. The 1,058 twelve-crate unmatched records are not classified beyond that slice. Widening the join is therefore not the lever on the five-crate slice; an expression-level seam model is the candidate, and whether it is the only path at the boundary is not established. Campaign sequencing follows: characterize, then change the instrument, then measure the population - never change instrument and population in one window. Characterization is done on one slice, so the instrument change is a candidate next step, not a settled one.
- **A bar only a new capability can reach is a capability bar.** When the measured gap to a bar is dominated by a class the instrument has no vocabulary for, repair work cannot close it and moving the bar is re-baselining. The honest options are a scoped claim with the boundary published, or the capability. Measured 2026-11-14 on the five-crate slice: 28.3% against a 50% bar, with at most +2.2 points available from repair and +34.6 from the unrepresentable class, both conditional. At the twelve-crate boundary the joined share is 26.3% and the unmatched class is 1,058, unclassified.
- **The calibration population is a build with a screening cost, not a join (measured 2026-11-14).** The two populations the record said had "never been joined" cannot be joined: `benchmarks/rust_corpus` (34 repositories) and `benchmarks/mutation_spot_check` (12 crates) share **zero** repositories, so the first calibration slice is a new corpus build, not a merge of two inventories. Measured on 7 of the 34 curated pins with local cargo-mutants 26.1.2 (CI pins 27.1.0) under today's toolchain, `--list` counts, no mutation run: whole-crate mutants are `anyhow` 176 (test suite 24s), `fd` 521 (39s), `bat` 1181 (122s), `thiserror` 12 (81s), `rustc-serialize` 1018 (its own suite exits 101 at the pin), `iron` 0 (suite exits 101), `winreg` 0. Brief 52's 27.1.0 measured runs read `fd` 503 and `bat` 1,132, so the 26.1.2 `--list` counts are an upper enumeration, not the measured population. The diff-scoped shortcut is dead: `cargo mutants --in-diff` over each pin's own behavior-change diff yields 0, 0, 0, 7 and 11 mutants on five of them, because a real change often touches code cargo-mutants does not mutate - too sparse to reach a scoring sample. Consequences for sequencing: (a) every candidate repository needs a screening pass first - build and test green at the pin, non-trivial mutable surface - and three of the seven screened fail it outright; (b) cost is mutants x suite time, so `bat` alone is ~38 CPU-hours serial while `anyhow` + `fd` together are ~7 CPU-hours serial (~2 at 4 jobs); (c) `anyhow` + `fd` + `bat` = 1,811 mutants (Brief 52's 27.1.0 measured runs; the 26.1.2 `--list` enumeration read 1,878), about 77% of the twelve-crate boundary's 2,360 (the often-quoted 1,745 is a five-crate subset, not the boundary). So a **population swap at constant sample size** is affordable on real workspaces: the same instrument, three repositories that are not the analyzer's own source, for a fraction of the compute the corpus conversation assumes. That is the cheapest test of the recorded risk that a pure-logic crate population flatters precision. It is a screening-and-cost fact, not a ruling on the slice.
- **The calibration campaign's first slice is machine-hours, and it now has a carrier (#14716, opened 2026-11-14T14:56Z).** The real-workspace population is a new corpus build, not a merge of two inventories, and it is the one long-lead item on the horizon that is work rather than a decision. The earlier "no carrier" reading was true at 14:49Z and is superseded: #14716 carries anyhow + fd + bat (1,811 mutants) and is the item that must begin before the campaign does, not with it. `mutation-spot-check.yml` remains manual-dispatch only by design, so a carrier is not yet a schedule; whether and when it runs is the orchestrator's.
- **Real-workspace precision is workspace-dependent; the named population is 0.714 at n=3 (measured 2026-11-14, Research Briefs 48, 51, 52 and 53; supersedes the n=2 and substitute readings).** Four real workspaces now have mutation labels. The intended population is `anyhow` + `fd` + `bat`: `anyhow` 1.000 (1/1), recall 0.511, coverage 0.068, owner tier 0/2; `fd` (pin `ce97e473`, fd-find 10.5.0) 1.000 (3/3), recall 0.670, coverage 0.266, owner tier 1/3; `bat` (WSL Linux, pin `4987f76`) **0.600 (6/10)**, recall 0.587, coverage 0.254, owner tier 0/4. **Pooled 10/14 = 0.714**, 25.4 points below the five-crate 0.968 (61/63) and 23.6 points below the 0.95 bar. The substitute population `anyhow` + `prost` + `bat` is 33/37 = 0.892, and the four-workspace population `anyhow` + `prost` + `fd` + `bat` is 36/40 = 0.900; `prost` (`4104042b042`) is 1.000 (26/26), recall 0.514, coverage 0.387, no owner pick emitted. All three populations have the same four bat misses (`clap_app.rs:22` `&&`->`||`, `:253` `||`->`&&`, `lessopen.rs:20` `!` deleted), so the shortfall is bat's predicate flips, not the third workspace. Recall is the stable quantity (0.511-0.670 across the four populations); precision and the owner tier are not. The owner tier stays the real gap: 1/17 five-crate, 0/2 anyhow, 1/3 fd, 0/4 bat, none emitted for prost. `fd` is not blocked: the earlier screening failure was a `TMPDIR`-inside-checkout artifact, and at the same pin `cargo test` passes 156 unit + 118 integration twice with `TMPDIR` outside the checkout. `thiserror`/`rstest` were rejected at screening. Two consequences: the n=2 "37 points below" reading and the substitute-only "5 points below" reading are both superseded and must not be quoted, and the bat misses are concentrated enough to be a testable discrimination hypothesis - four overclaims, three sites, all predicate flips - rather than population noise. The pooled figures are a report, not a receipt: no committed receipt exists for any of the real workspaces, and the brief says not to publish them as a rate.
- **The precision denominator is the joined quarter, so no precision figure describes the mutation surface (measured 2026-11-14).** Scored coverage on the four real workspaces is 0.254, 0.068, 0.266 and 0.387 - precision is computed over 10, 12, 3 and 26 picked mutants out of 1,132, 176, 503 and 419. anyhow's 1.000 rests on 12 of 176 mutants and fd's on 3 of 503; a clean sheet over a small, join-selected subset is not evidence about the 93% it does not join. Combined with 26.3-28.3% join coverage on the frozen populations, the December calibration can produce a precision headline that is honest over a biased subsample and silent about the majority of mutations. So the published label must carry the denominator, not only the population.
- **The public precision bar is a pure-logic-crate figure, and the page's bar row does not say so (measured 2026-11-14).** `docs/PUBLIC_PROOF.md` row `trust.mutation_spot_check_precision` reads 96.8% (61/63) against a 95% bar and "meets the bar", with a provenance note naming the receipt but not the population's character: twelve small pure-logic crates. The page's caveat - "Rates describe this corpus only; they are not a population estimate" - sits in a "What the corpus does not claim" section far from the bar row. On the intended real-workspace population the measured precision is 0.600 / 1.000 / 1.000 by workspace, pooled 0.714 (10/14) at n=3 - below the 95% bar and 25.4 points below the five-crate rate - so a reader who takes the bar row as a product rate is over-reading it materially, and on the one weak workspace by 37 points. The substitute population (anyhow/prost/bat) reads 0.892 (33/37), still below the bar. This is not a re-baselining question: the bar stays, and the population and the denominator are disclosed. Whether the bar row carries that qualifier now, before the December calibration, is the owner's, because it changes a public product claim; the Steward recommendation is yes, because the page is public and this is the product's central claim. The rule already in this record for analyzer revision applies to population too: a product figure carries the population that produced it, and one measured on a different population is population-specific, not a product rate.

## (C) Adoption evidence

## Adoption evidence needs the population axis the calibration rule already requires (measured 2026-11-15)

The record requires a calibration population to contain code the instrument did not write. The adoption campaign has no such rule, and its one retained self-source row is also its one row in a deferred-language surface.

Measured from the live ledger and running table (#14669, #1693 comment 6837057364), 2026-11-15T01:5xZ:

- **2 distinct real tasks / 1 active week / 0 accepted improvements / 3 adjudicated findings, true-finding rate 1/3.** No row after 2026-11-12T19:45Z.
- **Row 1 is the instrument's own source.** ripr-swarm PR #14063 changed `crates/ripr/src/analysis/language/python/*` - the analyzer's Python reach/ownership code - and ripr graded a test in that change `weakly_exposed`; the discrimination replay ruled it a false weak (predicate-specific per-invocation admission asymmetry). The task is ripr reading a change to ripr's own analyzer.
- **Row 1 is also the only non-Rust surface in the sample.** The standing non-goal defers language breadth until recall, repair follow-through and speed improve. So the campaign's single self-source row, its single false finding and its single deferred-language row are the same row.
- **Row 2c is genuine external code** (perl-lsp-swarm, `literal_scan.rs`, a Rust implementation), and it produced both the true finding and a second false weak.

Two consequences, neither a ruling:

- **`1/3` is not a rate on either axis the record already uses elsewhere.** It pools a self-measurement with an external-code measurement, and it pools Rust with a deferred surface. The same objection the record raises against a calibration slice taken from the analyzer's own repair surface applies one campaign over: a false finding produced while the instrument reads itself measures the instrument's defect, not the product's discrimination.
- **Sourcing has a language bias that the non-goal makes material.** ripr-swarm's change traffic is concentrated in its own analysis code, much of it non-Rust, because that is where the repository is being developed. A campaign that sources tasks from its own repository will therefore accumulate evidence about the surface it has explicitly said is not where the value lies. Perl-lsp-swarm is the corrective source, not the balance-the-pair source.

Steward recommendation, not a ruling: the adoption rate is reported split by **population** (`self_source` / `external`) and by **language** (Rust / other), in the ledger row and in the Dec 31 verdict. The ledger schema is #14669's and the verdict carrier is #1693's; the durable rule is only that the split must exist wherever the rate is published, because a pooled rate hides both axes.

Also standing, verified 2026-11-15: the bounded placement rule this record names as the lever for the #14062 false weak is **not in flight**. #14116's live candidate is disclosure-only ("retains the first `IncludeReach::Workspace` limitation and ... changes the refusal to explain"), and #14707 is a different slice (a file's own module glob beside `std::thread_local!`). So the class that refuses `assert_eq!` credit across `crates/ripr` is being named, not fixed, and the adoption campaign's Rust tasks in that crate will keep meeting it.

## Adoption evidence has one supplier, and it is not the fleet (measured 2026-11-15)

The campaign's target is eight real behavior-changing tasks by 2026-12-31. Its evidence supply was never measured. Measured now, from live GitHub objects:

- **Real change traffic is not the constraint.** 579 merged PRs in `ripr-swarm` and 107 in `perl-lsp-swarm` in the seven days to 2026-11-15 (~98/day). The campaign has 2 tasks, both dated 2026-11-12, none since, and both ledger rows are `captured: recalled` (#14669).
- **Three candidate suppliers, one demonstrated.** (a) The owner's discretionary use produced both rows. (b) Agents offered ripr as optional ran it in **0 of 3** runs (#13050, n=3, one model, installed 0.10.0 - the issue itself calls this a lead, not a rate). (c) Real PR traffic has never been sampled: no mechanical PR-head lane exists, and the measurement lanes (`pilot-measure`, `pilot-ranking`, `outcome-nightly`) run fixtures and pinned diffs, not incoming PR heads.

Two consequences, neither a ruling:

- **The count is a statement about the owner's week, and the rate at n=3 is noise.** Both are honest and neither is a product claim. The Dec 31 verdict will therefore be uninformative for a supply reason, not a value reason - the same shape as the count-before-value trap, one layer down.
- **The rate is fleet-producible at bounded cost, and the count is not.** `ripr check --format agent --committed` emits one recommendation per run (row 1's full-format check was 306 s and 82 findings; the agent format is the bounded unit). A pre-registered sample of N merged PR heads, stratified by language, with one adjudicated item per PR, yields a true-finding rate with a published denominator. The cost is adjudication, not analysis, so the sample size is set by how many adjudications are affordable, not by machine time.

Durable rule: **a campaign whose evidence supply is one person's discretionary attention cannot be driven by the fleet.** Its rate must be sampled mechanically with a pre-registered denominator, or reported as an observation. A sample cannot be reconstructed at reconciliation, so it must be pre-registered before the window it measures - which is why this is a November item, not a December one.

**The unowned signal is #13050.** The end state is agent-ready test intent, and the only measurement of an agent choosing ripr when it is merely available is 0 of 3. That is a lead, not a rate, and it is the one number that decides whether the end state is reachable at all. It is not a feature gap to close with more surface; it is a product question about why the offered value is not chosen.

Steward recommendation, not a ruling: (a) the count stays owner-bound and is reported as self-use; (b) the rate gets a pre-registered mechanical sample now, before December, with the adjudication budget stated up front; (c) #13050's unprompted-use rate is the owner's product question, and the fleet should not answer it by adding surfaces. The ledger schema is #14669's, the verdict carrier is #1693's, and the sample design is the orchestrator's.

## (D) Surfaces, bars and the December verdict

## The calibration campaign measures a different surface from the one the product sells (measured 2026-11-15)

The record has a rule that a product figure carries the population that produced it and the analyzer revision that produced it. It is missing the third axis: the **surface**.

`ripr` has two discrimination surfaces, and the harness itself refuses to mix them. `xtask/src/reports/mutation_spot_check.rs:138` states it: the Rust span-join figures "score the same cargo-mutants mutants against repo-exposure seams", while `--rust-diff-mode` applies each mutant's own recorded diff to a scratch copy and runs `ripr check --diff` - "the product path" - and is "advisory and never mixed with the Rust span-join figures".

Every number the campaign currently plans to publish is the span join:

- The public precision row (`docs/PUBLIC_PROOF.md:58`, `:129`) is 96.8% (61/63) over canonical-precise `strongly_gripped` mutants - the seam/grip path, not `check --diff`.
- The real-workspace population (anyhow 1.000 1/1, fd 1.000 3/3, bat 0.600 6/10, pooled 0.714 10/14 per Brief 53) is recorded as "seam precision", i.e. the same span join.
- The adoption campaign's evidence is the other surface: row 1 and row 2c were produced by `ripr check --format agent --committed`, which is diff mode.

So the campaign that establishes the public claim measures repo-exposure seams, while the end state ("an LSP-native sidecar that watches changed code") and the adoption campaign's value are diff mode. Those are different instruments over the same mutants, and the harness says so in its own boundary text.

**No diff-mode figure exists on the real workspaces.** No committed receipt and no `docs/` or `metrics/` artifact carries one; the issue tracker was not exhaustively checked. `--rust-diff-mode` is implemented and no committed receipt or `docs/`/`metrics/` artifact records it against anyhow, fd or bat. The lane is a flag on the run #14716 is already doing, not a new build.

Why this is material rather than pedantic: the diff-mode path carries a guard the repo-exposure path does not. `changed_operands_are_never_evaluated` (`crates/ripr/src/analysis/classify/infection.rs:34`) fails closed when `same_connectives(after, before)` is false, and `before` is a diff-mode field. In repo scope there is no `before`, so the guard returns early. **All four of the intended population's overclaims are bat predicate-operator changes** (`clap_app.rs:22` `&&`->`||` plus a second operator mutant on `:22` inferred as `!` deleted, `:253` `||`->`&&`, `lessopen.rs:20` `!` deleted) - exactly the class that guard exists to catch - and anyhow and fd are 4 of 4. So the entire measured shortfall from the 0.968 five-crate figure to 0.714 is one workspace's predicate-operator overclaims, not a broad precision decay. **Hypothesis, not established:** the bat 0.600 may be a repo-exposure artifact that the product path does not reproduce. I did not run `--rust-diff-mode`, and I did not trace repo-scope probe construction to confirm `before` is always `None` there.

Two consequences, neither a ruling:

- **The December calibration can publish an honest number about the wrong surface.** If the headline is the span join, it describes the repo-exposure instrument; a reader will take it as the product's precision, because the public row already reads that way. The published label must name the surface, not only the population and the denominator.
- **The cheapest test is already built.** Adding `--rust-diff-mode` (bounded by `--max-mutants`) to the #14716 run yields both figures from the same mutants and the same machine hours. If the two agree, the surface axis is a disclosure; if they diverge, the campaign has found which instrument the public claim is actually about, before December rather than after.

Durable rule: **a product figure carries the surface that produced it.** Population, analyzer revision and surface are three axes; a figure that names two of them is still ambiguous, and the ambiguity runs in whichever direction flatters the product.

Steward recommendation, not a ruling: run `--rust-diff-mode` on the same three workspaces as part of #14716, and have the December verdict state which surface it claims. The lane, the cap and the receipt shape are the orchestrator's.

## The public precision bar and the R2 bar are two different numbers (measured 2026-11-15)

The public trust page and the release ladder disagree about the bar for the same metric, and the disagreement sits exactly at the measured value.

- `docs/PUBLIC_PROOF.md:58` reads "When ripr says a test discriminates, real mutants are caught | 96.8% | >= 95.0% | meets the bar".
- `docs/METRICS.md:58` (R2) reads "Precision of 'discriminator' claims at least 97% against real mutants".
- `docs/METRICS.md:107` (replaces cargo-mutants) reads "Precision | 96.8% (61 of 63) | 97% | no".
- The page's bar comes from `benchmarks/dx_scoreboard/scoreboards.toml` `trust.discriminator_claim_agreement` `target = 0.95`, set when the scoreboard was created (#5299) and never updated when the R2 ladder was defined (#13042). The replacement criterion's threshold is `0.97` (`xtask/src/reports/mutation_spot_check.rs:1526`).

So 96.8% is above the page's bar and below the R2 bar. The page says "meets the bar"; the R2 ladder and the replacement criterion say "no". The page is more flattering than the internal bar by two points, and the two points are the whole difference.

Why it is material rather than bookkeeping: the public page is the trust claim, and the record's honesty discipline says a public figure must not be more flattering than the internal one. A reader who takes "meets the bar" as the R2 verdict is over-reading it, and the December calibration will publish a real-workspace number (0.714 pooled, Brief 53) that is below both bars - so the page's "meets" is the last flattering reading before the honest one lands.

Durable rule: **one metric, one bar.** A public page and an internal ladder that name different thresholds for the same metric must be reconciled, or the page must name which bar it uses and why. A bar that is lower in public than in the ladder is a claim drift, not a display choice.

Steward recommendation, not a ruling: make 0.97 canonical (it is the R2 ladder and the replacement criterion), which flips the page row to "below the bar" and the page count from 29/21 to 28/22. This is the owner's because it changes a public product claim; the orchestrator owns the scoreboard lane but should not pick the number.

**Sequencing consequence (new):** the record plans for a December calibration that makes the claim honest, but not for the outcome where the honest number is below the bar. If the real-workspace population reads 0.714 (or any value below 0.95/0.97), the product fails R2 precision on the population that matters, and the campaign after calibration cannot be distribution - it must be precision/recall improvement. The record should state that fork now, so January does not start distributing a product that just measured below its own bar.

## December's verdict is already determined (measured 2026-11-15)

The calibration campaign is scheduled to publish a verdict in December. On numbers already measured, that verdict cannot be anything but `not_yet`: three of its four thresholded criteria already read below their bar on the intended population, and the fourth was unreachable before the run started.

| criterion | bar | intended population (Briefs 48/51/52/53) | status before any run |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| precision of discriminator claims | 0.97 | 0.714 pooled seam (10/14) | below |
| recall flagged-or-unknown | 0.80 | 0.511 / 0.670 / 0.587 | below |
| scored coverage | 0.50 | 0.254 / 0.068 / 0.266 | below |
| Python/TypeScript agreement | established | `not_established` | unreachable |

The criterion is population-blind by construction. `metrics/public-proof/mutation-spot-check.json` `replacement_criterion.claim_boundary` reads "Scope is Rust on the recorded crates and checkout revisions only", so feeding it the real workspaces produces the same rows over a different population, not a different verdict. And the non-goal bars instrument changes during a measurement month, so the run cannot move any of the three.

Two consequences, neither a ruling:

- **A verdict fixed before the measurement is not the campaign's outcome.** December can still add what no number currently has: a committed receipt (the real-workspace figures are a report, not a receipt), the denominator, the population label and the surface label. That is disclosure, and disclosure is the product. But if December is read as a pass attempt it reports failure on three axes it was forbidden to improve, and the one actionable finding - bat's four overclaims, three predicate-flip sites - is buried under them.
- **The bar that binds at December is agent-chosen, not the owner's.** `scored_coverage 0.50` carries `threshold_source: "agent-chosen: a majority of generated mutants must reach a canonical_precise seam join"`. It is the one thresholded criterion with no capability behind it and no owner call, and it is already known to fail. An agent-chosen bar should not be able to determine a published verdict; it belongs beside the verdict as a capability gap, which is what this record already calls it.

Steward recommendation, not a ruling: pre-register December's success condition as the two things the run can actually decide - (a) a committed real-population receipt carrying population, surface and denominator, and (b) the surface hypothesis, whether `--rust-diff-mode` reproduces bat's 0.600, since all four bat misses are predicate-operator changes and the diff-mode guard `changed_operands_are_never_evaluated` fails closed on exactly that class. Pre-register the fork with it: precision at or above the bar on the product surface means the claim stands and distribution follows; below means a precision/recall campaign and the public row re-scoped to the population where it holds.

Durable rule: **a measurement campaign must name the decision it changes before it runs, and must be able to change it.** If every thresholded outcome is already known, the campaign is disclosure - legitimate, but it must be labelled disclosure, or its failure will be read as a product failure.

## (E) The editor action surface is fail-closed (measured 2026-11-15)

The end state is an LSP-native sidecar, and the LSP is not a stub: `crates/ripr/src/lsp/` is about 4 MB of source across ~60 modules (`backend.rs` 648 KB, `diagnostics.rs` 383 KB, `state.rs` 235 KB, `tests.rs` 1.4 MB), with a lane (`docs/lanes/LANE_3_EDITOR_LSP.md`), a cockpit report in `ci.yml`, and a closed editor-evidence closeout. So the delivery vehicle the vision names exists and is owned.

The question that matters for the precision finding is whether that surface turns a wrong finding into a wrong action. It does not, by construction:

- `crates/ripr/src/lsp/actions.rs:1808-1811` requires `data.preview_actionability.repair_packet_ready == true` before a repair action is emittable, and `:2240` applies the same condition on the execution side, so an action that was enabled under an older payload cannot execute.
- `crates/ripr/src/lsp/repair_card.rs:27-39` returns `None` - omits the card entirely - when any producer fact cannot be bound, rather than rendering a partial card.
- `crates/ripr/src/lsp/action_contract.rs:169` is a fail-closed emit guard: a disabled action may only carry a reason, never a payload.
- The weaker action class is gated separately on `gap_state == "actionable"` (`lsp/gap_artifacts.rs:180`, used at `actions.rs:451` and `:634`), and that class is evidence collection - open the related test, copy the packet - not a repair.

Consequence: the measured precision shortfall (0.714 pooled on the intended real workspaces) is a **diagnostic-quality** problem at the point of reading, not an **action-safety** problem at the point of repair. "Three in ten claims are wrong" and "three in ten one-click repairs are wrong" are different exposures, and only the first is currently true. That is the reason the December verdict should be read as a precision/disclosure verdict rather than a product failure, and it is a fact the record's surface axis did not have.

Caveat: this is established from the code path and its fail-closed unit tests, not from an end-to-end trial. I did not run the LSP against a real workspace holding a known-wrong finding and observe the editor. A trial of that shape is the missing evidence, and it is cheap: one workspace, one known overclaim, one editor session.

## (F) Gate and landing-path corroboration

- **An eval baseline that no lane runs is a report, not a gate (measured 2026-11-14).** `benchmarks/agent_eval/baseline.json` is the regression reference for agent-facing output (`agent-brief`, `cli-agent-loop`, `cli-agent-find`), and no workflow invokes `cargo xtask agent-eval --compare`; the baseline was written at `84e04b2e` (#14335) and main is 213 commits past it at `09ccb6d683` (measured 2026-11-15T04:00Z). The first comparison (#14726) therefore reports six changes at once, mixing two improvements with one agent-visible defect (a duplicate gap row for one changed line). Two consequences: a "regression" against a 213-commit-old baseline is not evidence that any single PR regressed, and the agent-facing surface - the adoption campaign's actual value - has no enforced floor. The orchestrator owns whether a lane runs it; the durable rule is that an unenforced baseline must be read as a report, and its absence must not be read as "no regression".

- **Landing path is settled: the native merge queue is canonical and it is landing (owner, 2026-11-14T07:09Z).** The earlier "the queue never lands, direct squash is observed practice" premise was true when measured and is now false. Corroborated by queue landings on 2026-11-14: #14095 and #13899 at 07:04:09Z, #14547 at 07:53:29Z, #14502 at 09:18:15Z, #14559 at 10:14:14Z and #14565 at 11:21:11Z, each carrying `removed_from_merge_queue` by `github-merge-queue[bot]` at its merge second. `mergedBy: EffortlessSteven` is not evidence of a direct merge, because queue landings carry that actor too; the discriminator is the queue timeline event, not the PR's mergedBy field or the commit's parent count. The direct single-parent squash merges seen earlier were the owner's own manual landings, not a competing policy. The real cost is throughput, not correctness: roughly 47 minutes per `merge_group` run on the same `em-ci` pool the PR-head qualification uses, so admission rate is the orchestrator's lever, and a merge_group failure rate is a delivery diagnostic, never a campaign fact. Whether the queue *stays*, and its ruleset, remain the owner's settings decision; nothing here retires or reconfigures it. `merge-ready` and actual queue entries remain distinct states.
